articles.title: Autumn wreaths and ‘doorscaping’: why we need more life in our front gardens
articles.author: James Simpson, Lecturer in Landscape Architecture, University of Sheffield
paras: There was a time when decorative wreaths appeared on front doors in December, stayed on front doors for a few weeks, and then disappeared.
Now red and gold autumn wreaths and Halloween wreaths are popping up everywhere. These seasonal displays are part of a wider social media fashion for “doorscaping”.

It is easy to see the appeal. A wreath introduces colour, foliage and a little seasonal personality without much effort. But this enthusiasm for decorating the front door raises an interesting possibility: could it encourage people to pay more attention to the garden immediately below?

Choosing a wreath and choosing plants for a front garden can both be ways of making the entrance to a home more attractive. A study of 1,000 people in England found that creating something beautiful was one motivation for front gardening. People motivated by appearance also tended to have greener front gardens.
That does not mean wreath enthusiasts will necessarily become gardeners. But the same interest in seasonal colour and decoration could encourage some to try planting around their front door.
And British front gardens could benefit from more planting.

The Royal Horticultural Society’s 2025 mapping estimates that 55% of front-garden space in Britain is paved, compared with 36% of back-garden space. Earlier RHS research found that the proportion of completely paved front gardens tripled between 2005 and 2015, although subsequent surveys suggested some recovery in planting.

Parking is one reason. An Ipsos survey found that, among people with largely paved front gardens or driveways, 28% said they needed the space for cars, while 45% thought it was too small for plants. Front gardens also have to accommodate access, bins and the everyday demands of domestic life.
But the cumulative effect of paving matters. One driveway can seem negligible. A street of them is a landscape.

This is where the appeal of seasonal decoration becomes useful. The seasonal colours and foliage that make a wreath attractive could also be found in plants growing around the front door. Someone who enjoys decorating their entrance might also be tempted to extend that interest into the garden.

A reused container, a few bulbs or a hardy perennial can be an inexpensive starting point. The RHS recommends containers for completely paved spaces, as well as climbers for walls and plants for otherwise unused corners.

Living plants do require some care. Pots need watering, and not everyone has the time, confidence or physical ability to maintain a garden. But starting with a few manageable plants offers a way to try growing something without committing to a complete redesign.

There may also be opportunities to go further. A strip beside a driveway or an unused corner could provide space for plants. Where practical, a few paving slabs could also be lifted to make room for planting. Parking and greenery do not have to be mutually exclusive.

These changes offer more than decoration. Flowers can provide nectar for insects, while shrubs and hedges offer shelter for wildlife. Larger plants, particularly trees and climbers, can provide shade and help keep buildings cooler in summer. Unlike impermeable paving, exposed soil and properly designed permeable surfaces can also help rainwater soak into the ground.

A study of more than 900 sites in front and back gardens and streets across England and Wales assessed combinations of grass, hedges, trees, shrubs and container plants. It found that mixtures of different plants generally performed better across several environmental measures, such as cooling or flood control, than just one type.
A pot of flowers cannot provide all these benefits, but it can still support insects and introduce planting where paving and parking have left little growing space.

Those decisions matter for new housing too. The 2026 Building for a Healthy Life design toolkit, a government guide to the design of housing developments, encourages space for planting in the front of houses.

But having space for plants is only part of the picture. People also need a reason to grow something. And this brings us back to the wreath. Its appeal lies in how easily people can add colour and character to the front of their homes.

If even some of that enthusiasm extended from the door to a pot, a border or a climbing plant, our streets could become more attractive and better for wildlife. If that interest grew to include more trees, shrubs and planted ground, it could also help our neighbourhoods cope better with heat and heavy rain.
What starts as a little seasonal decoration might become a lasting interest in growing plants.

articles.title: When climate data is transformed into visuals some people and places get overlooked
articles.author: Monika Frątczak, Postdoctoral Researcher, Digital Technologies, Communication and Artificial Intelligence, Manchester Metropolitan University
paras: When a climate disaster happens, people thousands of miles away may encounter it through numbers: how many people died, how many were displaced, how many homes were destroyed and how much infrastructure was damaged. But for the people living through it, the disaster is not a dataset. It is a home, a family, a livelihood and a place.
Billions of people around the world live in places and situations that are highly vulnerable to climate change, such as parts of Africa, Asia and small Pacific islands.

Data visualisations have become an important way of communicating climate change. Warming is represented through colours, emissions through lines and bars, and floods and fires through maps and animations. These visualisations can make an enormous and complicated problem easier to understand, but they can also shape how people feel about it.
Crucially, some visualisations don’t tell the full story.

I explored this in my new research with 34 social media users in the UK and Poland. I showed participants climate data visualisations and asked them how they felt and what they did with the information. Participants described worry, fear, sadness, anger and concern, but also curiosity, surprise and pleasure suggesting that visualisation can make unpalatable data more enjoyable.

The warming stripes for Poland (above) is a visualisation that shows temperature changes through coloured stripes. One participant said this visualisation looked “so pretty, nice and interesting”. But once they understood what the colours represented (red for warm temperatures; blue for cooler temperatures), their reaction changed, and the image became upsetting. The visualisation did more than show climate change: it changed how the participant experienced it.
What data visualisation leaves out

One of the most revealing moments in my research came from a meteorologist from Tonga who used to live in the UK. They first saw the warming stripes visualisation shared on social media, but Tonga was not shown as a location. They commented on the visualisation, asking whether stripes could be created for Tonga. They wanted to see what was happening at the scale of individual islands. They then went to the interactive version, where users can select locations to create their own stripes, but they could not create one for Tonga because the data wasn’t accessible for specific islands.

The visualisation showed temperature changes across broad regions, including the Pacific. But the participant wanted to see what was happening at the scale of particular islands. That visualisation prompted them to think about what could be done. They shared it with colleagues, and they decided to reproduce something similar using their own data.

The problem was not that the global visualisation was inaccurate. It was that accuracy at a global scale did not guarantee visibility at a local one. For communities such as those on Tonga (an island that contributes only a fraction of global emissions yet bears the brunt of climate change), this local visibility matters.

So who are visualisations making climate change “visible” for? For the participant from Tonga, climate change is closely connected to land, the sea, community and everyday life. They explained that data visualisation needs to reflect local context yet engage audiences more widely to convey an urgent need for climate action.
What happens after seeing the data

Climate data visualisation is not just a technical exercise. Researchers usually ask whether a graph is accurate, clear and easy to understand. But we should also ask who is represented, who is missing and whose experience the data allows us to see.

What people see can shape how they feel about climate change and what they believe they can do about it. My research found that emotional responses could lead people to share information, discuss it with others, change their everyday practices and sometimes inspire more formal political engagement.

But strong emotions did not automatically lead to action. People were more likely to describe taking direct climate action when they also felt there was something they could actually do at a local or national level. A sense of agency can help determine what happens after people encounter climate information.

The challenge for climate communication is not simply to find better and more accurate ways of showing the scale of the crisis. It is to ask whether, when climate change gets transformed into data, audiences are still able to see the people behind the numbers – and whether what is being shown gives people not only a reason to care, but a sense of what they can do.
Making climate change visible is only the first step. The harder and more critical challenge is considering whose experiences we see, whose are left out, and what happens after we see them.
Monika Frątczak receives funding from UKRI/ESRC.

articles.title: Chiricahua is the nation’s newest national park – what does that mean?
articles.author: Seth T. Kannarr, Visiting Honors Lecturer, Southern Illinois University Edwardsville
paras: With a stroke of a pen, President Donald Trump has officially created the United States’ 64th national park.

Chiricahua, in southeastern Arizona, was established as a national monument in April 1924 to protect its towering rhyolite hoodoos – tall spires of rock – and diversity of wildlife. The mountainous landscape is commonly known as a “wonderland of rocks.”

An act of Congress, signed by Trump, has now designated the 12,000-acre property a national park, the flagship label of the National Park Service system. It joins the Grand Canyon, Petrified Forest and Saguaro as the fourth national park in Arizona.

As a geographer who studies parks and the naming of places, I have seen that when a National Park Service property is redesignated as a national park, the new label doesn’t typically include much change for the site itself beyond signs and branding.

There’s not usually more money available to manage or protect the site. But the new title serves political purposes and could mean quite a lot to visitors, supporters and surrounding communities alike in the coming years.

The National Park Service manages 433 properties, which it calls units, with 19 different designations, such as “national battlefields,” “national lakeshores” and “national scenic trails.” Only 64 of these units carry the formal title or designation of “national park.”
All but one of these categories can be bestowed only by Congress. National monuments can be created by the president directly, under the provisions of the Antiquities Act of 1906.

For example, the Antiquities Act has been at the center of a decade-long controversy over the size of Bears Ears National Monument, which President Barack Obama created to protect 1.3 million acres in Utah in December 2016. That same act allowed Trump to shrink the protected area to 200,000 acres in 2017 and President Joe Biden to reexpand it to 1.3 million acres in 2021. In 2026, Trump slashed it again, to 121,000 acres.
Why redesignations make a difference

My previous analysis of the contentious redesignation of the Jefferson National Expansion Memorial in St. Louis to Gateway Arch National Park in 2018 found that it was not done to offer additional protection for this monument to the United States’ Western exploration and growth.
Rather, the move was meant to take advantage of the public significance of the “national park” label and thereby attract more tourists and tourism revenue to the local economy.

The effort to make it a national park was part of a local campaign to renovate the underground visitor center, revitalize the park grounds and increase tourism. But the law that formalized the change included no additional funding, resources or protections for the Gateway Arch.

Changing the designation contradicted the park service’s own declaration that the term “national park” should be used for an area that “contains a variety of resources and encompasses large land or water areas to help provide adequate protection of the resources.”

During congressional hearings, the deputy director of the National Park Service, Robert Vogel, recommended the Gateway Arch not be labeled a national park but rather a national monument, because it “is too small and limited in the range of resources the site protects and interprets to be called a national park.”

Gateway Arch National Park is now the smallest-area park in the U.S., at less than 200 acres, and is home to a large steel arch, an open lawn area, a museum and a single historic building – a courthouse where one of the Dred Scott trials was heard, along with other civil rights cases.

However, it does not provide opportunities to view wildlife in its natural habitat, spectacular geologic features, diverse outdoor recreation opportunities or a sense of wilderness that the public has come to expect from national parks.
The park’s website admits “it is unusual for a national park to have no natural plant life” and describes the park as adjacent to the “concrete jungle of downtown St. Louis.”

Although Chiricahua’s rocky landscapes and archaeological evidence of long-standing Indigenous use and occupation more closely resembles what many people expect for a national park, it likely will receive some of the same public critique that the Gateway Arch and other national parks redesignated during the first Trump administration have received.
Potential ‘new’ national parks on the horizon
In rare cases, a community, group or other organization proposes adding an area that is not currently managed by the National Park Service to the system, but that process takes a lot of time.
It is more common to change the formal designation of a property already within the system, as has happened with this redesignation of Chiricahua.

Similarly, Indiana Dunes National Lakeshore became Indiana Dunes National Park in 2019. That same year, White Sands National Monument in New Mexico became White Sands National Park. And in 2020, New River Gorge National River in West Virginia became New River Gorge National Park and Preserve.

There are redesignation efforts underway seeking to make national parks in other locations as well, including the Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area in New Jersey and Pennsylvania, Apostle Islands National Lakeshore in Wisconsin, and Rock Creek Park in the District of Columbia.
In my measure, it is simply a waiting game to see whether these National Park Service sites will also be redesignated to national parks.
What will actually change for Chiricahua?

Making Chiricahua a national park was a bipartisan effort – co-sponsored by Arizona U.S. Reps. Juan Ciscomani, a Republican, and Greg Stanton, a Democrat – that has received some opposition for several reasons.

The complaints have highlighted fears that the new label will bring increased tourism and overcrowding in what is considered a small park with limited infrastructure. Now that Chiricahua has been redesignated, the potential influx of new visitors in the coming years could affect the more personal and isolated experience that they currently appreciate.

However, the only real changes in these places would be in marketing – the signs, brochures and merchandise sold in gift shops. But these changes have an important effect: The tagline of “new national park” markets well to potential visitors.

But the funding that Chiricahua receives from the federal government will not change, and the label of “national park” won’t actually protect this landscape any better than it already is under the stewardship of the National Park Service.
This article includes material previously published in an article about the potential redesignation of Ocmulgee Mounds on Dec. 8, 2025.

articles.title: El Niño is threatening California’s fragile coast again – the 1982-83 El Niño opened eyes to the serious erosion risks
articles.author: Gary Griggs, Distinguished Professor of Earth & Planetary Sciences, University of California, Santa Cruz
paras: California’s coastal bluffs and beaches look rugged, but they can be surprisingly fragile in the face of a powerful El Niño.

The state saw that in 1982-83, when storms amid one of the most destructive El Niño winters in California history battered the coastline with powerful waves and torrential rain, leaving hundreds of millions of dollars in damage in its wake. The storms coincided with elevated sea levels, high astronomical tides and very large waves delivered by repeated storms.

Extreme waves that winter destroyed one-third of the Santa Monica Pier and tore off large sections of the Huntington Beach Pier and the Paradise Cove Pier, while also damaging the Seal Beach, San Clemente and Malibu piers. Numerous seawalls, decks and stairways were torn apart, and 33 oceanfront homes were destroyed.
Massive waves also stripped millions of cubic yards of sand from Southern California beaches, and sections of the Pacific Coast Highway suffered severe flooding, mudslides and washouts.

Along the central coast, waves and high-tide flooding eroded bluffs. In Pacifica, just outside San Francisco, the edge of a sandy cliff lost over 65 feet as it failed, collapsing onto the beach and forcing the relocation of a two-story building and removal of an entire row of mobile homes. This area of high but weak bluffs continued to erode over the subsequent decades, forcing the demolition of bluff-top homes and apartments.

The El Niño now building in 2026-27 is forecast to be even stronger, and coastal homes are already seeing damage. I have studied coastal geology and oceanography in California for nearly six decades. With the conditions expected this year, coastal flooding, coastal erosion and landslides are likely, and more dramatic cliff collapses wouldn’t be a surprise, though every El Niño is different.
What is El Niño and why is it so destructive?

El Niño is one end of a climate pattern that swings from warm to cold every few years and can change weather patterns around the world. Normally dry areas can experience flooding rains, and wet areas can suffer droughts. The U.S. Pacific Coast in particular can take a beating from powerful atmospheric river storms with heavy downpours.

El Niños begin with a shift in wind patterns, which normally push warm waters from east to west along the equator. For reasons still not fully understood, the trade winds die and the warm pool of water in the western Pacific begins to flow back toward the coast of South America.
Part of this warm mass moves north toward the coast of California as a pulse or bulge, known as a Kelvin wave, and it begins to have far-ranging impacts.

Seawater expands as it warms, which raises sea level along the Pacific Coast for weeks during these periodic events. While all El Niños are not created equal, during the very large 1982-83 event, sea levels were elevated above predicted high tides by about a foot in San Diego to nearly 2 feet in San Francisco.
These higher sea levels can reach higher elevations and last longer.

The elevated sea levels also allow storm waves to break closer to the shoreline, eroding beaches and bluffs, leading to damage and destruction of both private oceanfront development and public infrastructure, including streets and highways, bridges and piers, and parks and recreational facilities.
Why California is vulnerable
Much of California’s coastal and shoreline development took place from the late 1940s to the late 1970s when the state’s population exploded.
Homes were built on beaches, bluffs and dunes during a period when the coastal storm climate was generally mild and there were no real concerns with coastal hazards and future sea-level rise.
This changed quickly in 1978 when the first strong El Niño in recent memory arrived, raising alarm about the hazards ocean development was exposed to.

The extreme 1982-83 El Niño that followed a few years later caused about US$328 million (in 2025 dollars) in damage to oceanfront property, $87 million in losses to recreational facilities such as piers, parking lots and access stairs, and $66 million in damage to large engineering structures such as breakwaters and jetties designed to protect harbors from storm waves.

At least in the short term, the 1982-83 El Niño winter changed popular perceptions of the stability or security of oceanfront homes and other shoreline development. Building restrictions were tightened, insurance rates rose, and many requests for new seawall permits were submitted.
But then it was back to business as usual, as new arrivals to the coast outbid each other for the same oceanfront homes damaged a few years before.

Increased coastal armoring, such as seawalls and rock revetments, helped limit erosion during other very large El Niños that followed, in 1997-98 and 2015-16, along with lucky timing that large waves arrived at low points in the monthly tidal cycle, leading to significantly less property damage than in 1982-83.

The coast was not so fortunate in winter 2022-23, when high seas and waves alone caused an estimated $4.7 billion in economic losses along California’s coast. The simultaneous occurrence of large storm waves, high tides and elevated sea levels were almost identical to the El Niño conditions in early 1983, 40 years earlier.
The state’s latest climate assessment, released Oct. 19, 2026, warns of more intense storms and increased erosion as temperatures increase and sea level continues to rise.
What will California see in 2026-27?

The southern end of the state is already suffering wave damage from an exceptionally busy Pacific hurricane season, also fueled by El Niño. Swells have stripped away beaches and destroyed homes near San Diego. The state’s storm season, when powerful atmospheric rivers bring downpours, typically begins in October or November and runs through early spring.
The magnitude of the emerging 2026-27 El Niño, likely to be one of the strongest on record, is making clear that coastal communities need to adapt now to a very different future.
How each coastal neighborhood, city and county responds will vary depending upon their local conditions and vulnerability to coastal erosion and flooding.

While many communities are stockpiling sandbags, clearing culverts and preparing evacuation plans, there are limits on what they can do to stop erosion. Building seawalls and rock revetments can provide some protection if well designed, but they can also create new problems, including leading to the loss of beaches over time as sea levels continue to rise. Putting more sand on beaches is costly and very short-lived.

Extensive shoreline development, eroding bluffs, aging infrastructure and increasing exposure to extreme weather are placing growing pressure on coastal communities and shorelines around the world. Some will eventually face the difficult transition from continued shoreline protection to retreating from the coast – either planned retreat or following repeated damage.

There is little that any developed coastal area can do at this point to minimize the impacts of the El Niño underway. What they can do is prepare to manage the risks and try to adapt to the changing future.

articles.title: Hot and cold climate extremes push UK’s energy system to its limits, new report reveals
articles.author: James Mollard, Researcher, School of Geosciences, University of Edinburgh
paras: The arrival of cooler weather following a summer of heatwaves, is a timely reminder that the UK electricity system must be resilient to the effects of temperature extremes at both ends of the thermometer.
The Royal Meteorological Society has released a new report that highlights how recent weather conditions have influenced electricity generation, demand and the infrastructure that connects them.

Authored by experts from the society, the Met Office and multiple UK universities, the State of the Climate for the UK Energy Sector Report 2025-26 shows that more energy is being provided by weather-dependent renewable sources. But high and low temperatures will continue to put the energy grid’s capacity and infrastructure to the test.

Data from the National Energy System Operator (Neso) shows that renewable energy formed a higher percentage of overall energy generated in the UK over the reporting period (April 2025 – March 2026) than any other year on record. The proportion coming from the combination of solar and wind increased, providing more than 38% of the nation’s electricity. The proportion of gas-powered generation reduced to 25%.

However, the report highlights how extreme weather tests the resilience of the grid. The conditions that lead to very high and low temperatures create different challenges through increasing electricity demand, limiting generation and damaging network infrastructure. The UK’s energy network is having to adapt to cope with increasingly extreme temperatures. In cold conditions, the network is put under strain due to increased heating demand. This requires more energy at short notice, increasing reliance on non-renewable sources.
For those responsible for balancing the electricity system, including Neso, these weather extremes can create operational challenges. This makes it harder to match energy supply with demand.

In early January 2026, strong northerly winds brought cold Arctic air, snow and ice into large parts of the UK. Initially these winds provided up to 20 gigawatts (GW) of power towards the system, a significant proportion of the demand.

But as the freeze reached its peak on the evening of January 6, the wind died down and wind generation fell to less than a quarter of the levels seen in the preceding days. Simultaneously, electricity demand peaked, with the increase in heating needs seeing demand peak an additional 5GW higher than the previous day.

Electricity supply and demand have to be kept in balance in real time. When demand rises or available generation falls, the energy system operator can maintain that balance by using additional generators to increase their output, for example. On this occasion, gas-powered electrical generation filled the gap by providing more than 25GW to the system at it’s peak.

This meant the demand was comfortably met, but this was an expensive strategy that meant the operator was paying up to £700 per megawatt-hour (MWh) for this generation. This was due to the higher cost of turning to gas generation, and the need for additional generation at short notice which costs more than generation that can be planned further in advance. This compares to the usual rate of just over £100 per MWh for the rest of January.
At the other end of the spectrum, hot temperatures are increasingly becoming more of a concern for the sector.

The summer of 2025 was the warmest on record at the time, with temperatures 1.51°C higher than average. During warmer temperatures, the network operator often limits the amount of power that transmission lines carry around the country to prevent components overheating. This reduces the risk of lines expanding more with heat which would make them sag and potentially short out on nearby vegetation or structures beneath.

Nevertheless, several faults in the network were attributed to heat causing infrastructure damage, leading to power cuts across parts of England, especially during two periods of heatwaves that occurred at the end of June and start of July.

In Europe, where temperatures also spiked, nuclear power plants were forced to limit output or shut down altogether because the water used to cool them with, taken from nearby rivers, was too warm. Increased temperatures and below-average rainfall also increased fire risks. The largest area lost to wildfire burning in the UK since satellite records began included a “mega-fire” in Scotland. Several of these fires led to localised power cuts across the country.
Preparing for future extremes

The UK’s new grid upgrade plan from the government, which aims to expand and modernise the British grid system to allow for connections to new generation sources and upgrades of current infrastructure, needs to consider the consequences of extreme temperatures. This includes ensuring that upgraded infrastructure can withstand the extreme heat we are now seeing more regularly in UK summers, as well as ensuring that capacity for transmission of electricity from generation sources to population centres is increased.

Delays to electricity grid upgrades risk higher consumer bills as the operator is required to pay wind farms to stop generating because electricity produced cannot be be carried to where it is needed, replacing it with more local gas-powered generation instead.

The resilience of the UK grid has stood up well to the challenges it faced from the weather in the past year. But maintaining that resilience requires continued investment and adaptation as the climate, energy needs of the nation and profile of energy generation all continue to change.

articles.title: Wild fish are a precious resource – here’s how aquaculture can bolster food security
articles.author: Wesley Malcorps, Research Fellow, Institute of Aquaculture, University of Stirling
paras: Small fish such as sardinella are an affordable source of protein and essential nutrients for millions of people across West Africa.

Some of these fish are increasingly exported or processed into fishmeal and fish oil for aquaculture feeds used in high-income European countries and across East Asia, particularly China. As nutrient deficiencies are common in people living in parts of West Africa, retaining more fish for local consumption could help improve diets and address dietary health problems.

Aquaculture is one of the world’s fastest-growing food production sectors. Despite its growth in the last three decades, global wild fish catches for marine ingredients have declined overall. Production has increased in some regions, including West Africa, but the overall decline is mainly due to improved fishery management that allows recovery of fish stocks.

Globally, a quarter of wild-caught fish are processed into fishmeal and fish oil, and only a small share originates from West Africa. Most is used in animal feed, with aquaculture accounting for the largest share. These provide valuable nutrients, particularly in early-life-stage diets and for carnivorous species such as salmon and shrimp, while contributing to the relatively low carbon footprint of farmed seafood.

The supply of marine ingredients is highly regulated and fairly stable but should not be taken for granted. Climate change and warming periods such as El Niño can weaken the upwelling of nutrient-rich waters from the deep sea. This reduces the availability of plankton and fish and limits the supply of marine ingredients required for aquaculture.

This means we need to make the best use of the resources already available. Fish processing by-products (including heads, guts and skeletons) are playing an increasingly important role, accounting for 34% of global fishmeal production and 54% of fish oil supply in 2024.
A new era of supply chain risk

Marine ingredients from potentially unsustainable sources have slipped through the net despite responsible sourcing claims. One 2025 investigation found that certified Turkish-farmed seabass sold by major retailers in Europe was fed fishmeal sourced from three factories in Senegal that have been linked to food insecurity and job losses in local communities.

One way to reduce risk in aquaculture feed supply chains is to source ingredients domestically. But this is easier said than done. Aquafeed supply chains are dependent on the global trade in marine and terrestrial ingredients and thus face challenges related to scale, cost, nutritional quality and environmental sustainability.

While marine ingredients can be sustainably sourced and continue to be essential to the global food system, it’s important to use them in efficient ways that maximise their contribution to human nutrition. Certification programmes currently focus on ensuring that fish are caught or farmed responsibly. The environmental and social safeguards include stock status, environmental footprint and making sure workers are treated fairly.

The certification programmes pay less attention to food security and critics argue they favour export markets and corporations over local communities. As a result, calls are growing for broader measures of what constitutes truly sustainable and ethical seafood.

Some scientists argue that fish, such as anchovies and mackerel, provide more essential nutrients when eaten directly rather than used as feed. Most species used in the marine ingredients industry have low market appeal and limited consumer demand, meaning that diverting fish from feed to food does not automatically improve food security.

Peru’s anchoveta fishery is the world’s largest fish stock used to produce marine ingredients. Despite its scale and nutritional value, there has been low demand for anchoveta as a food fish within Peru. Factors such as low demand, short shelf life, limited logistics and strong economic incentives to process fish into fishmeal and fish oil have often hindered the development of markets for some fish as food. Strategic use of some fish as feed can help convert marine resources into nutritious and accessible seafood.

To make the most of limited marine resources, the aquaculture industry could improve how it tracks fish and nutrients as they are transformed into farmed seafood. We have developed a novel peer-reviewed performance tool that provides a common sustainability language. At the heart of the tool is the Fish In: Fish Out (Fifo) ratio, a measure of how efficiently fish, and the omega-3 fatty acids they contain, are converted into farmed fish.

Efficiency can be improved by increasing the use of fish processing by-products that are not normally eaten by people and by strategically replacing certain marine ingredients with alternatives such as algal oil and insect meal. The tool is currently being used by a variety of organisations like feed and ingredient companies, farmers, environmental charities, and researchers.

Applying the tool in our latest study already challenged conventional thinking about marine ingredient use in aquaculture. Although Faroese salmon is often viewed as a major consumer of marine ingredients, we found it was actually a net producer of edible omega-3 fatty acids. This was achieved by upcycling valuable nutrients from inedible sources (fishery by-products) into a nutritious farmed product, without increasing the need for fish that could be consumed directly by humans.

Making the most of limited marine resources is important, but decisions made in one country can affect food availability and affordability elsewhere. Therefore, harmonising nutrition-sensitive policies across local, national and regional levels is crucial to achieve meaningful outcomes. Traceability systems can play an important role, but they must do more than track supply chains.

They can only make a meaningful difference when they empower local communities through greater participation in decision-making and improved market access. They should support those closest to the resource, rather than treating them simply as sources of data for downstream companies. In West Africa, this could include retaining a proportion of the catch for local consumption and improving the cold chain to support its distribution.

These approaches would enable the marine ingredients and aquaculture industries to operate effectively. They would also contribute more to global food security, the economy and the supply of nutritious seafood to consumers.

Wesley Malcorps is Co-Founder and CEO of Blue Food Performance and provides consulting services to the seafood sector, including the development of sustainability assessments, strategies, dashboards and tools. articles.title: Jackdaw approval: what a new North Sea gasfield means for UK energy security, bills and tax
articles.author: Karl Matikonis, Assistant Professor in Taxation, University College Dublin
paras: The UK government has just approved the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea, clearing the way for production to begin as early as this winter.
Jackdaw, around 150 miles east of Aberdeen, could account for roughly 6.5% of UK North Sea gas production at its peak and will connect to existing infrastructure at the Shearwater platform.
But what will this actually mean for households and public finances? Will Jackdaw lower energy bills? Probably not by any noticeable amount.

Producing more British gas may sound as though it should lower prices. But North Sea gas is not reserved for British consumers at a special domestic price. It is sold into a market connected to Europe and influenced by international gas prices. This was clear following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Britain continued producing gas domestically, yet consumers were still exposed to soaring international wholesale prices.

According to one analysis, even if Britain maximised North Sea production and returned all resulting government revenues to households, the average annual saving would be no more than £82. Jackdaw is one field, so its effect would be small.
Will this new gas field licence improve energy security? Here the case is stronger.

Britain consumes more gas than it produces and increasingly depends on imports as older North Sea fields decline. Jackdaw will not make Britain energy independent, but additional domestic production can reduce imports.

There is an important distinction between security of supply and protection from high prices. Jackdaw can contribute to the first, but not the second while consumers remain exposed to international gas prices.

In terms of how much tax Jackdaw will generate, North Sea taxes are currently charged on profits, not total sales. Investment reliefs (tax breaks that allow companies to deduct certain investment costs) can reduce those taxable profits.

Companies can generally deduct day-to-day operating costs when calculating taxable profits. They can also claim tax relief for certain development costs, investments to reduce emissions and, eventually, the costs of dismantling the field.

For Jackdaw, development investment will be in the region of £2.1 billion according to Adura, the UK North Sea’s largest independent oil and gas producer. Yet using the developer’s production forecast which estimates of how much gas and other products Jackdaw will produce each year, and the UK government’s Office for Budget Responsibility’s March 2026 oil and gas price assumptions, we estimate Jackdaw would generate only around £1.5 billion to £1.6 billion in gross sales by the end of 2029. Around £1 billion would come from gas, with the remainder from condensate and natural gas liquids (these are the liquid products extracted alongside natural gas that are sold separately).
Based on this simple comparison, gross sales through 2029 would still be below the project’s implied development investment, even before operating costs are taken into account.

This does not mean Jackdaw will pay no tax. Public information does not reveal how much investment qualifies for tax relief, when allowances will be used or how Jackdaw fits into the operator’s wider North Sea tax position. Adura estimates that Jackdaw and the much larger Rosebank project together could generate around £1.4 billion in tax by mid-2029 but does not say how much of that would come from Jackdaw.

There is another complication. The energy profits levy (a temporary 38% tax on oil and gas profits) is due to end by March 2030. It will be replaced by the oil and gas revenue levy, a new tax that would apply when oil and gas prices rise above specified levels. Unlike the current windfall tax, this would charge 35% on revenues above specified price thresholds, regardless of a field’s costs. My research suggests the same revenue threshold can affect high- and low-cost fields very differently.
What Jackdaw really changes

Jackdaw will not give Britain cheap gas or make the country energy independent. Its significance is more limited: it can replace some imported gas and support economic activity, but Britain will remain exposed to international gas prices.

The financial picture is similarly complicated. A 78% headline tax rate does not mean 78% of Jackdaw’s revenues will reach the Treasury. Investment reliefs can reduce tax in a field’s early years, while jobs and supply-chain activity generate other tax revenues and eventual decommissioning costs can also qualify for tax relief.

These benefits must be weighed against the emissions and environmental costs of further fossil-fuel production, and against investing instead in renewables, storage and other ways of reducing dependence on gas.
By producing a little more of its own gas, Britain can marginally improve its security of energy supply, but this won’t lower prices or guarantee an immediate tax windfall.

articles.title: Who should have a say in which species are saved? The California condor offers lessons for a global biodiversity treaty
articles.author: Shannon Gibson, Professor of Environmental Studies, Political Science and International Relations, USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences
paras: In 1987, biologists captured the last free-flying condor to transfer it to captivity, and the largest flying North American bird species was officially declared extinct in the wild. Today, after decades of coordinated efforts and millions of dollars spent on captive breeding and reintroduction efforts, more than 300 condors have been restored to their natural environment.
It was a victory for the species’ survival, yet this triumph was contested at nearly every step of the way.

Conservationists fought bitterly over whether trapping every bird should be considered rescue or surrender. Critics argued that the cost was better spent on other threatened species. Rural communities in Utah and Arizona raised concerns about federal land-use restrictions. Hunting groups such as the National Rifle Association opposed bans on lead ammunition, a leading cause of condor deaths.
The condor’s comeback illustrates several questions that governments and conservation organizations grapple with today, including which species get funded and who bears the costs.
These are some of the questions being discussed at the U.N. Convention on Biological Diversity conference, being held Oct. 19-30, 2026, in Yerevan, Armenia.

In 2022, countries worldwide adopted an agreement at that year’s biodiversity conference to halt and reverse biodiversity loss, known as the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. It includes goals to raise US$200 billion a year from public and private sources around the world by 2030 to conserve and manage at least 30% of the world’s land, coastal areas and oceans, stop human-caused extinctions and help struggling species survive.
The agreement itself doesn’t choose which species to save, but its rules are designed to shape national conservation priorities and guide the funds that pay for conservation.

Saving a species like the condor affects local communities and businesses whose activities have put those species at risk. Without local buy-in, pouring money into recovery efforts can fail, yet local communities are often left out of the discussions.
Deciding which species deserve protection
An estimated 1 million species are currently threatened with extinction worldwide, and early assessments suggest the world is falling short on most of the agreement’s global biodiversity targets.

Because resources are limited, conservationists must weigh trade-offs in deciding which species to protect and how. Should they fund expensive rescue efforts for a species close to extinction, or interventions likely to help multiple species at once? Or maybe they should protect organisms that are unique to a specific geographic region or a species that sustains local livelihoods.

Some species are valued for what they do for humanity, such as pollinating crops or purifying water, known as ecosystem services. Honeybees, for example, pollinate over $15 billion worth of crops in the U.S. alone each year. Others hold cultural and spiritual significance, as the condor does for the Yurok Tribe in California. Many conservationists argue that living species possess an inherent right to exist independent of their usefulness to human beings.

Getting support for measures to save charismatic species can be easier than for others, however. Think of Greenpeace’s “save the whales” campaign or the World Wildlife Fund’s panda logo. A panda’s adorable face can help pay for its protection and potentially the protection of its surrounding habitat, helping other species living there.

A 2025 study examined more than 14,000 species-focused conservation projects from 1992 to 2016. Five mammal groups – primates, carnivores, whales, elephants and rhinos – received 86% of available funding, despite accounting for only one-third of threatened mammal projects. Plants and invertebrates, which are crucial for pollination, nutrient cycling and sustaining food webs, received only 6.6% of the financial backing.

Conservation groups and economists at the Paulson Institute estimate that the world needs to spend an additional $1.3 trillion annually on biodiversity conservation and restoration to stop and reverse biodiversity loss.
At the 2026 biodiversity conference, delegates will also take up another question that can make or break species recovery: When conservation affects local people, who pays and who gets a say?

While conservationists celebrated efforts to return wolves to Europe over the past two decades, some farmers lost livestock to these predators and faced higher costs to protect their flocks. Current European Union funding programs help support livestock protection, but farmers’ ability to shape wolf recovery is part of the story too.

Conservation can go terribly wrong if local communities aren’t consulted during planning. In the Ngorongoro Conservation Area, a protected area in Tanzania, the Maasai have fought for years against government orders that they leave the land they have lived on for generations in the name of lion conservation. In March 2026, two presidential commissions recommended that the evictions continue in order to protect wildlife, in a process that included few Maasai, Indigenous peoples’ advocates at the Oakland Institute reported.

Protecting vulnerable species often means also supporting the communities living alongside them. At the last round of biodiversity talks in 2024, countries created a permanent advisory body to bring Indigenous peoples and local communities’ knowledge and decisions into the treaty’s decisions.

At this year’s conference, known as COP17, they must agree on how that advisory body will operate, including whether these communities get a formal role in decision-making. They are also expected to adopt guidelines for how the 30% global conservation targets apply in Indigenous territories.

The international agreement can’t dictate what happens on the ground, but its rules shape national conservation priorities and guide the funds that pay for conservation. That is why the debate over local consultation is at the heart of the 2026 talks. Conservation that is designed for people, rather than with them, risks losing the trust and local cooperation that makes recovery last.

Two key issues at the conference involve guaranteeing that Indigenous peoples and local communities have a say in decisions on their territory, including how conservation programs are designed and how resources are allocated.

The global biodiversity framework calls for a “whole-of-society” approach, recognizing that protecting nature needs more than government action alone. But participation is not the same as decision-making power.

Advocates for Indigenous groups say communities are too often consulted after priorities are set, rather than being involved in setting them. Whether the farmer paying for fencing or the Indigenous community with connections to a species helps set priorities or is only asked for input after the project has been approved shows whether consultation is genuine or not.

The condor’s return shows that nearly extinct species can recover with help. But sustaining a species’ recovery requires protecting the conditions – and supporting the people – that make their survival possible.
Researcher Garrett Ordonez, an environmental studies and international relations student at USC, contributed to this article.

articles.title: Is it wrong to kill wild animals that attack humans? Sometimes conservation demands it
articles.author: Adam Hart, Professor of Conservation Ecology, University of Gloucestershire
paras: When an Amur tiger recently killed a man at Yorkshire Wildlife Park in northern England, the park announced that the tiger would not be killed.
Days later, a 71-year-old fisherman was killed by an alligator in Florida in the US. This time, the animal was captured and killed.

Two fatal attacks, but two very different responses. The distinction is not simply between a tiger in captivity and an alligator in the wild. It is about whether killing an animal can prevent further harm.

Sometimes removing a dangerous animal is necessary to protect human life. More surprisingly, it can also protect other wildlife, by preventing people retaliating against animals who weren’t involved in the original attack.

A tiger attacking someone who enters its enclosure is behaving like a tiger, and killing it would achieve nothing. Removing an animal posing an ongoing threat is different. But in Yorkshire, the tiger remains behind barriers designed to keep people safe. The fatal encounter needs investigating, but the problem was that a person got in, not that a tiger got out. Killing the tiger would not address any potential failures in enclosure security.

The Florida alligator presents a different problem. There is no good evidence that crocodilians develop a particular taste for human flesh after an attack, but they can become accustomed to people and learn to associate human activity with food, potentially increasing the risk of further encounters.

Where an animal poses a continuing threat, removing it may be justified on safety grounds, although a fatal attack alone does not establish that killing it was necessary. For communities that depend on crocodile-inhabited rivers for fishing, washing or collecting water, simply telling people to avoid them may not be realistic.

In Borneo, a fatal attack by a false gharial, a large and threatened relative of crocodiles, prompted a search for the animal responsible. A large male was killed, but examination of its stomach failed to establish that it was responsible.
Following another fatal attack, a second false gharial was killed, this time with the victim’s remains in its stomach. No further crocodilians were killed following that incident.

The consequences of indiscriminate retaliation can be devastating. In 2018, after a man was killed by a crocodile at a breeding facility in West Papua, Indonesia, an angry crowd entered the facility and killed all 292 crocodiles kept there, including hundreds of animals that had played no part in the attack.

When people fear that a dangerous animal remains a threat, the pressure to act can be considerable. If authorities fail to respond, communities may take matters into their own hands, killing animals uninvolved in the attack. Identifying and removing the responsible individual can sometimes prevent this escalation and protect other wildlife.

But targeted removal is not straightforward, not least because identifying the right animal can be difficult. In addition, involvement in a fatal attack does not necessarily mean an individual is unusually dangerous. The circumstances may explain what happened, and killing the animal may do little to prevent another attack.

Such retaliation is not confined to crocodiles. In India in 2024, villagers near Ranthambore tiger reserve killed a tiger following the death of a shepherd. That year, a leopard that injured four people in Karnataka, south-west India, was beaten to death by a crowd, despite wildlife officials attempting to capture it.

Retaliation also occurs when lions kill livestock. In Kenya in 2015, herders poisoned a cow carcass after lions killed their cattle. Three lions from the famous Marsh Pride died, along with 11 vultures.

The incident illustrates how livestock conflict can become a wider conservation problem. A timely, targeted response may be preferable to allowing fear and anger to escalate into indiscriminate killing.

Often, better barriers, safer access to water or changes in how people encounter wildlife offer more lasting solutions. Providing safe water, for example, reduces the need to enter crocodile-inhabited rivers. Killing an animal should never be a substitute for addressing the circumstances that made an attack possible.

For people living alongside dangerous wildlife, these are not abstract conservation dilemmas. Expecting communities to tolerate serious risks without effective protection is neither reasonable nor fair. Those communities also need a meaningful say in how dangerous animals are managed. Decisions made solely by distant authorities or conservation organisations can overlook both the risks people face and the practical options available to them.

Equally, killing an animal does not necessarily make anyone safer. Decisions should depend on whether removal is likely to reduce danger and protect other wildlife. Sometimes killing a dangerous animal is justified, not despite conservation concerns, but because of them.

articles.title: Subsidence claims: after drought, ground can shrink, swell or even collapse when it rains – causing damage to homes
articles.author: Arya Assadi Langroudi, Senior Lecturer in Geotechnical Engineering, University of East London
paras: A crack appears beside a window after weeks of scorching weather. As much as you might hope the ground beneath your house will recover with the first rain, the effects of a dry summer can continue long after temperatures fall.

The UK is recovering from the hottest summer on record. The drought, however, has not simply disappeared. According to the Environment Agency, south-east England received 61% of its normal September rainfall, leaving its soil moisture deficit around twice the seasonal average.

The financial consequences are staggering. After the UK’s 2022 heatwave, insurers recorded 18,000 claims from homeowners in the second half of that year for subsidence (the gradual sinking of the ground surface).

In 2025, domestic subsidence payouts reached £307 million, 10% above 2024 figures. Between April and June 2026, the average paid claim reached £20,000. Although payouts include repair costs, the amount shows the scale of the damage to houses by climate change.

Clay-rich soils commonly lose water and contract during drought. If that happens unevenly beneath a foundation, one part of a house may settle further than another, producing cracks in its walls. Trees may intensify local drying as their thirsty roots extract water from the ground.

When rain replenishes moisture, some clays swell again, potentially pushing foundations upward. The recovery, however, is neither complete nor instantaneous. A heavy shower may wet the surface without restoring moisture several metres below ground, and different parts of a building may move at different rates.

Cycles of drought and rain can displace salt and sticky clays within sandy soils and clay-like silty soils. While that displacement generally makes these soils stiffer, it can also make them susceptible to sudden subsidence when large volumes of water flow through the pores opened up after the summer drought, weakening the contacts holding the grains apart.

These soils can show problems normally associated with “collapsible soils”, which are explored in my 2019 study of English loess, a fine, wind-blown silty sediment that’s very porous. My research shows that seemingly similar silty soils can behave quite differently, depending on how they formed and how their particles became arranged and bonded over time. Some layers are better at supporting loads than others.

Where soils are susceptible to collapse once wet, rapid subsidence may be further escalated by a leaking drain or poorly sited soakaway (an underground drainage system that collects surface rainwater, stores it and allows for it to slowly seep out). That is one of the principal reasons the British Geological Survey (BGS) advises maintaining water pipes and keeping soakaways further from buildings where loosely cemented soils and soluble rocks may be present.

Two houses on the same street may not respond in the same way. Their foundations may reach different depths or sit on different soil layers. The ground beneath one garden may be shaded by trees, while the next has been paved over. Rainwater can be diverted by a driveway, concentrated by a leaking pipe, or drawn away by roots.
A geological map can flag a potential hazard, but it cannot tell a homeowner whether a particular crack is caused by ground movement. The building, soil and local water conditions all affect that.
Soil is not simply a platform for foundations. Its pores store nutrients and water for plants, lock carbon, carry rain towards groundwater and provide habitats for roots, fungi and earthworms.

Roots are part of the soil’s plumbing. They create pathways for water and hold particles in place. If drought damages fine roots or kills vegetation, the ground may absorb rainfall differently, while its surface becomes more exposed to erosion.

A 2025 review of drought-affected soil studies by the BGS describes how drying may reduce microbial and earthworm activity, weaken soil structure and expose bare ground as plants die back. This makes some soils at a greater risk of erosion by the runoff when rain returns. Soil staying wet for a long time, combined with intense rainfall can increase the erosion risk.

Soil degradation, loss and erosion can affect the food security. In the 2026 harvest survey, UK wheat yields were around 11% below their five-year average and spring barley around 17% below. Some crops like oilseed rape, enjoyed higher yield. The contrasting yields mark why one harsh summer does not produce one uniform outcome across the landscape.

So what should homeowners do to manage the problem? Many fine plaster cracks are cosmetic. New or widening diagonal cracks, cracks visible inside and outside, suddenly sticking doors or distorted floors merit closer attention. Photograph them with a ruler and date, check that gutters and drains are sound, and seek advice from your insurer and a qualified surveyor if movement appears to be progressing. Do not rush to remove a mature tree: it may change the moisture balance and create a different problem.

The longer-term outlook makes better ground management urgent. The BGS estimates that, by 2070, more than 1.8 million British properties could be in areas where clay is particularly prone to shrinking and swelling. This figure assumes a medium level of future greenhouse gas emissions. If emissions remain high, the number could rise to 4.2 million properties are at risk. This does not mean all these homes will suffer damage. The figures identify potentially vulnerable ground, rather than predict actual subsidence. They also exclude other hazards, such as the sudden collapse of some soils once flooded.

Protecting homes is not just about building stronger foundations. It calls for careful drainage, sensible land and tree management plus healthy soils that can retain and carry water without creating new hazards elsewhere.
Arya Assadi Langroudi receives funding from Royal Academy of Engineering.

articles.title: The driveway divide: why parking for electric vehicles is such a big barrier
articles.author: Bernardino D'Amico, Professor, School of Computing, Engineering and the Built Environment, Edinburgh Napier University
paras: Most people who have an electric car have access to a driveway or private parking. In England, 90% EV owners can park easily and charge theirs from home. But roughly 40% of UK households don’t have off-street parking, so the question is how they would charge an EV and would easy access to home-charging influence their decision to acquire one.

The practical problems are well documented. In a block of flats or a tenement, installing an EV charger may not be an option due to the cost and the legal consent required from third parties who may have no interest in giving it. In a block of flats, installing an EV charger can also be difficult because it may require running cables from the flat’s electricity supply to a shared parking space, if one is available, or to the street where the vehicle is parked.

This can involve drilling through walls, installing cables through shared areas of the building and altering existing electrical infrastructure. Such work is generally more complex (and costly) than in a detached house, where a charger can usually be installed on an external wall close to the property’s electricity supply.

According to the Electric Vehicle Association, a non-profit representing EV drivers in England, 87% of EV owners with driveways say their car is cheaper to run than a petrol or diesel equivalent. Among those without, only half say the same because they have to default to more expensive public chargers.

As a researcher exploring effective designs for urban environments, I’ve been looking at whether fixing this home-charging gap would solve the problem of access. I found that the driveway divide is really less about infrastructure and actually more about wealth in disguise.

My colleagues and I looked at data on Scottish households. Our latest study suggests that having a driveway does not get you into the electric car market – money does. A driveway only helps once you are already in.

We linked nationally representative Scottish household and housing data sets, capturing variables such as income, work, dwelling home type and age, and whether anyone there already owns or intends to buy an EV. Then we built a causal model: think of it as a map of factors that genuinely influence each other.

Wealthier households are far more likely to live in a house that comes with a driveway and to also have the financial means to buy an electric car. A standard statistical model cannot tell those two things apart. It will simply report that driveways and electric cars “go together” or correlate, leaving researchers like me to guess why.

Our approach let us ask a question you cannot normally answer from survey data: what would actually change if a household suddenly had a private driveway, holding everything else the same? The answer surprised us.

Having a driveway does make a difference. It raises the probability of owning an electric car by 70%, a substantial jump for a group (the EV owners) that is relatively small to begin with. Immediate intent to buy an EV rises too, but almost all of that effect lands on households already thinking about buying an electric car at some point in the future. A driveway pushes people along a journey they had already started.

For the roughly half of Scottish households not considering to buy an electric car at all, a driveway changes almost nothing. Income, on the other hand, is different: when we simulated what would happen if a household earned more, the share of households not considering buying an electric car fell by 23%, that is more than ten times the apparent driveway effect on that group.

The contrast is stark: money opens the door, a driveway walks you to the till. The two factors operate at different stages, which explains something that has puzzled researchers. Electric car uptake has been slowest among people in flats and tenements, and the natural conclusion has been that home charging is the problem. Our findings suggest that is only true for people already considering to buy an EV, whether sooner or later.

A Glasgow tenement household that has decided to go electric but has nowhere to charge from home faces a real infrastructural barrier. For a household on a modest income that has never seriously considered buying an electric car, the main barrier may instead be the upfront cost. Although average advertised prices for new EVs have recently fallen below those of petrol cars, this does not mean that comparable cars cost the same. At the more affordable end of the market, new EVs still tend to be less affordable than new petrol or diesel cars.
Making street charging more accessible or public charging cheaper could help households who can afford an EV. It would not, however, solve the problem of being able to afford one in the first place.

All of this points to a two-track policy response. For households outside the EV market, the priority is affordability: a stronger used electric car market, and financial support aimed at those who need it rather than those already buying in. For households already intending to buy but stuck without a driveway, home-charging access is the binding constraint.

Scotland is already piloting cross-pavement charging, which runs a cable gully under the pavement so a car parked on the street can be charged from the house. The Scottish government has also consulted on relaxing planning rules to make on-street charging easier.

The driveway divide is real, but it also involves a wealth divide. Any equitable transition needs to tackle both. Investing in home-charging infrastructure alone will mainly benefit the people who were already going to buy an electric car anyway.

articles.title: Federal spending on climate change before 2024 election boosted incumbents of both parties
articles.author: Kayla Morton, Assistant Professor of Blue Economy and Policy, University of Delaware
paras: A massive federal spending effort to combat climate change passed in 2022 without a single Republican vote in the U.S. House or the Senate. But the billions of dollars it authorized benefited Republican and Democratic politicians alike – so long as they were already in the House of Representatives – according to an analysis I conducted with several fellow researchers. The results suggest that incumbents can still reap electoral rewards when federal money reaches their districts, even if they opposed the bill that provided it.

Enacted in 2022, the Inflation Reduction Act squeaked through the Senate only through a tiebreaking vote cast by Vice President Kamala Harris. It authorized spending US$370 billion to combat climate change and lower greenhouse gas emissions, primarily through subsidies such as a tax credit of up to $7,500 for buying an electric vehicle and incentives for making commercial buildings more energy efficient, rather than by imposing new fees or taxes.
Before the 2024 election, over $204 billion had been spent on clean energy projects around the country, through a combination of private investment and federal incentives.
While Republicans opposed the legislation, 79% of the law’s investment went to Republican congressional districts.

Even when Republicans vote against climate legislation at the national level, at least some favor investing in clean energy technology at the state and local level, because those investments bring local economic benefits. Many Republican districts, which are often large and more rural, are well suited to these kinds of projects.
Benefits of federal investment

Elected officials are sometimes accused of “pork barrel politics,” seeking to direct federal taxpayer spending to their own congressional districts. In part that’s because voters see federal investment as creating local jobs and stimulating economic growth.

Although no Republican voted for the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022, some Republican lawmakers began defending parts of the law as investments reached their districts. In August 2024, heading into the election, 18 Republican House members urged House Speaker Mike Johnson to preserve the law’s clean energy tax credits, which they said “created good jobs in many parts of the country – including many districts represented by members of our conference.”

That support continued after the election. In March 2025, after Republicans retained control of the House and party leaders began considering cuts to the law’s programs, even more Republican House members called for preserving the clean energy tax credits, which could be used, for example, to finance a large wind energy project or construction of a battery factory. The lawmakers argued that repealing the credits while major projects were still under construction would jeopardize investments already underway and the jobs tied to them.
The bill’s funding affected the 2024 election
Our analysis finds that Inflation Reduction Act funding helped incumbent House members of both parties in the 2024 election.

During the campaign, both Democrats and Republicans highlighted benefits of the investments funded by the act. Republicans usually used language like “economic development opportunities,” while Democrats directly mentioned the act itself.

Some districts got nothing, and one got nearly $8 billion. Some of the largest investments were in Republican-held districts in North Carolina and Georgia to expand capacity at electric vehicle plants already under construction. These companies were eligible for corporate tax breaks from the law and hoped to benefit from increased consumer demand because of the law’s tax credit for people purchasing electric vehicles.

In Mississippi’s 2nd Congressional District, which got $588 million in funding from the Inflation Reduction Act, Rep. Bennie Thompson, a Democrat, received 61.8% of the vote in 2024, up from 60% in 2022. In Michigan’s 5th District, which got almost $2 billion under the law, Rep. Tim Walberg, a Republican, received 65.7% of the vote in 2024, up from 62% in 2022.
We found that the more money a representative’s district got from the Inflation Reduction Act, the more the candidate improved their electoral performance in 2024 over how they had done in 2022.

When we conducted our statistical analysis, we accounted for multiple factors that could influence election results, including the district’s support for Trump, the incumbent’s previous vote share, campaign spending and district demographics. Using statistical methods to isolate the effects of Inflation Reduction Act funding, we found that doubling the amount of federal investment in a congressional district led to about a 0.9 percentage-point increase in the incumbent’s 2024 vote share relative to their 2022 result.

Our analysis showed that both Democratic and Republican incumbents saw electoral benefits from Inflation Reduction Act investment, even though Republicans in Congress had universally opposed the legislation. While some incumbents still lost votes or their seats, the data showed that greater Inflation Reduction Act investment helped them perform better than they otherwise would have.
These results indicate that voters may respond more to the money coming into their districts than to the underlying purpose of that funding.

While previous federal spending projects helped incumbent House members in elections, we found no direct evidence that district economies improved between 2022 and 2024. Instead, it’s more likely that incumbents claiming credit for the investments on the campaign trail explained why election results improved with Inflation Reduction Act funding. The lesson is that voters pay attention to actual or promised investments that might come into their areas.
Dismantling the subsidies and tax breaks

Upon taking office in 2025, the Trump administration and the Republican majority in the House rolled back many of the law’s climate provisions. A massive package of tax breaks and spending cuts sometimes referred to as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” removed tax credits for energy efficiency improvements and electric vehicle purchases.
The Trump administration has also moved to expand fossil fuel production on federal lands.

This evidence indicates that presidential priorities can outweigh even direct benefits to House members on highly polarized issues. The fact that some climate-related tax credits remained even after passage of the big budget bill does indicate that economic development policies may remain appealing to Republican leadership.

These electoral benefits indicate voters may reward investments even when the policies that created them remain politically contentious. Economic investments in fighting climate change can generate local political benefits across party lines, even if those benefits are not enough to overcome national divisions over climate change.
This article is based on research conducted with Nives Dolsak, Inhwan Ko, and Aseem Prakash.
